name: Visigothic Kingdom
summary: A Germanic kingdom founded in south-west Gaul after the Visigoths sacked Rome (410); pushed into Spain, it ruled from Toledo until the Arab–Berber conquest of 711.

knownFor.label: Sack of Rome
knownFor.note: By Alaric before the kingdom was founded.

knownFor.label: Visigothic Code
knownFor.note: One law for Goths and Romans.

location.value: Toledo was capital from 542 to 711 in the infobox, with Barcelona serving temporarily from 507 to 542; the page does not give a date for the move.

terrain.value: Meseta plateau, mountains and river valleys.

climate.value: Mediterranean on the coast, with continental heat and cold on the central plateau.

resources.value: Grain, olives and wine, plus metals such as gold, silver, iron and copper.

disasters.value: Plague from 542 and repeated famines weakened Hispania.

population.value: The page gives no population figures; it says the Gothic–Roman distinction had largely disappeared by the late 6th century. The entry’s 4–6 million and 200,000 are unconfirmed.

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural; a few walled towns and a royal or ducal capital.

disease.value: Plague outbreaks, above all the Black Death (1347–51).

migration.value: Goths moved from Gaul into Spain after defeat at Vouillé (507).

economicBase.value: Farming on Roman-style estates (latifundia) worked by dependent peasants and the enslaved.

tradeRoutes.value: Mediterranean trade, mostly with the Byzantine Empire and North Africa, through ports such as Cartagena.

wealth.value: Wealth rested on the land owned by a Gothic and Roman aristocracy and on the king’s share of taxes.

inequality.value: Nobles and clergy above peasants, many of them serfs.

governmentType.value: An elective monarchy: the page says the monarchy took on a completely elective character with the fall of the Balti.

keyRulers.value: Liuvigild reigned 569–586; the royal family’s conversion to Catholicism under Recared came in 587, and he announced the Nicene creed at the Third Council of Toledo in 589.

succession.value: Kings elected by nobles and bishops; many murdered.

institutions.value: The Visigothic Code, completed in 654, ended the old tradition of separate laws for Hispano-Romans and Visigoths.

stability.value: Frequent coups and civil wars; kings were often overthrown or murdered.

eliteConflict.value: Noble factions fighting over the throne.

armyAndTech.value: Noble war bands and cavalry formed the army, and the king could call up free men.

majorWars.value: Alaric II was killed at the Battle of Campus Vogladensis near Poitiers in 507 and Toulouse was sacked; by 508 only Septimania was left in Gaul.

territoryChange.value: Lost most of Gaul to the Franks after the Battle of Vouillé (507) and moved the capital to Toledo.

alliancesRivals.value: The Franks and the Byzantines (who held southern Spain for a time) were rivals; the Suebi in the north-west were conquered in 585.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded, but the Visigoths made fine metalwork and issued a law code (Liber Iudiciorum).

scienceEducation.value: Isidore of Seville’s Etymologies, a key medieval encyclopedia.

openness.value: Open to trade; closed to rival faiths at times.

communicationTransport.value: Roman roads, rivers and coastal shipping continued to be used.

religion.value: Arian Christianity until 589, then Catholic; Reccared’s conversion is dated 587 in one passage and 589 in another, and the Third Council of Toledo in 589 denounced Arianism.

languageWriting.value: Latin was used for law and the Church; the Goths’ own language faded and left few traces.

artsArchitecture.value: Small stone churches (San Juan de Baños).

socialStructure.value: Gothic nobles, Hispano-Roman landowners, peasants, slaves; Jews persecuted.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the king, the Catholic Church and the land, as Goths and Hispano-Romans slowly merged.

dailyLife.value: Village farming; bread, porridge and beer or wine.

neighbours.value: The Franks, the Suebi, the Byzantines, the Basques and, by the end, the Muslim world across the Strait.

ideasReligions.value: King Reccared’s conversion from Arian to Catholic Christianity (589) united the Goths and Hispano-Romans.

colonisation.value: The Goths took over Roman Hispania, with imperial permission at first.

riseSignals.value: Alaric’s Visigoths sacked Rome in 410; in 418 Honorius rewarded King Wallia’s federates with land in the Garonne valley, and the kingdom was based at Toulouse (418–507 in the infobox).

peakPeriod.value: By the end of his reign Liuvigild (568/9–586) had united the whole Iberian peninsula, conquering the Suebic Kingdom in 585; the kingdom covered 600,000 km² in 580.

declineSignals.value: Civil war in 710 and the Arab–Berber invasion of 711 ended the kingdom.

outcome.value: A battle at the Guadalete River in late July 711 ended with King Roderic killed; most of the kingdom was taken by Umayyad troops between 711 and 719, and the infobox gives 721 for the Umayyad occupation of Septimania.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and charters; population figures are estimates.
